frames.narration: The login service writes one structured event per sign-in: time, user, source, outcome, request id. Before the line is written, password, token and card fields are redacted, so the log never holds a secret. Events are shipped off the host at once.

A fast attacker guesses passwords at 8 per minute from one source. A rule of 3 failures in 5 minutes fires at once. But the same rule also fires on mistyped passwords and on the office address, 36 alerts in the day, 30 of them false.

One engineer takes each alert for about 10 minutes, so alerts queue and the real one waits behind false ones. The engineer starts to ignore the channel. Alert fatigue is a detection failure that happens after the rule has fired.

Overcorrect: raise the threshold to 20 failures in 5 minutes. The queue is nearly empty, with 1 alert in the day. The fast attacker is still caught, but the slow one, at one attempt a minute, never reaches 20 in 5 minutes and is never detected.

A better rule uses a 60 minute window with a threshold of 40. It fires on the slow attacker 39 minutes in, long before the login succeeds, and is silent on the office. Detection is only the start: containment is the clock that ends the attacker's access.

A runbook shortens the last step: triage, then a scripted block of the source instead of working out how. On the fast attacker, containment falls from 29 minutes after the start to 16, and the access window from 19 minutes to 6.

Break it: block automatically on the noisy rule. The attacker is stopped 2 minutes in, but the rule also fires on the office address after a password reset, and 40 real people are locked out. Run a new rule in alert-only mode first. Afterwards, hold a blameless review of the timeline and fix the gaps it shows.
